## Abstract

This report analyzes the DuckDB fork to locate the areas where the tagma coordinate engine, implemented in C++ under `sw/cpp`, can contribute an innovative performance improvement. The analysis follows the two measured precedents that define the pattern. The CERN ROOT-Coord work replaced per-read index traversal with closed-form coordinate arithmetic over a per-axis mixed radix, measuring 69 to 181 times on an index-traversal-dominated I/O path. The ExaVerif CVA6 work enumerated the valid encoding subspace instead of the full space, measuring about 700 times at 0.6 percent density with an O(V) over O(N) scaling. The DuckDB fork documents the exact gap the lattice fills: the table scan path falls back to a full scan for any multi-filter query or compound index, stated as a FIXME in `TableScanInitGlobal`. The analysis ranks four integration areas, specifies the syntagma core upgrade scope that the integration requires, and sets the measurement plan. The immediate next step is the profile gate with the installed DuckDB package, which runs without a C++ build.

## The precedents that define the pattern

The CERN ROOT-Coord report measured the read path of the TTree columnar format. The production signature is 372,000 singular reads averaging 4.6 KB at an effective 33 KB/s. The coordinate store replaced branch, basket, and cache traversal with closed-form arithmetic over a per-axis mixed radix $(R, L, E)$: the linear index of a record is $n(r, \ell, e) = (rL + \ell)E + e$, and the byte offset is $\omega = n \cdot s$ with no hash and no index scan. The same medium completed the full file read in 2.79 s against 192.8 s, a 69.0 times gain, and 1.06 s when mapped, a 181.7 times gain, after a one-time conversion of 226.3 s that breaks even within the second pass. The stable claims are the request count and the system call count, which are media-independent.

The ExaVerif CVA6 report measured the structural pipeline of the verification engine. The standard path evaluates the full encoding space in O(N); the structural path enumerates the valid subspace in O(V) with a lazy odometer over topologically ordered fields and O(1) re-fix maps. The measured speedup follows approximately $k/D$ where $D = V/N$ is the valid density: the CVA6 full space at 0.6 percent density measures about 700 times, and the gain is algorithmic, not linguistic. Both reports applied the same discipline: a profile gate before implementation, a measured baseline, a one-time conversion cost, and correctness verification.

The two LLM tracks bound the expectation. The vLLM and llama.cpp KV measurements returned parity because the block-table and cell-index indirection was a negligible share of the compute. The boundary between the compute-dominated LLM domain and the scan-or-index-dominated database domain is the reason the DuckDB track proceeds: the indirection and the scan are the dominant costs in the multi-dimensional point and range query path.

## The DuckDB integration surface

The fork analysis identifies four areas, ranked by expected impact and integration risk.

### Multi-filter index gap

`TableScanInitGlobal` in `src/function/table/table_scan.cpp` decides between a full table scan and an index scan. It restricts the index scan to exactly one filter and a single-column ART, and documents the multi-filter case as a FIXME:

```duckdb/src/function/table/table_scan.cpp#L746-755
	// FIXME: We currently only support scanning one ART with one filter.
	// If multiple filters exist, i.e., a = 11 AND b = 24, we need to
	// 1.	1.1. Find + scan one ART for a = 11.
	//		1.2. Find + scan one ART for b = 24.
	//		1.3. Return the intersecting row IDs.
	// 2. (Reorder and) scan a single ART with a compound key of (a, b).
	if (filter_set.FilterCount() != 1) {
		return DuckTableScanInitGlobal(context, input, storage, bind_data);
	}
```

The compound ART path is also rejected earlier in `TryScanIndex`:

```duckdb/src/function/table/table_scan.cpp#L708-718
bool TryScanIndex(ART &art, IndexEntry &entry, const ColumnList &column_list, TableFunctionInitInput &input,
                  TableFilterSet &filter_set, idx_t max_count, set<row_t> &row_ids) {
	// FIXME: No support for index scans on compound ARTs.
	// See note above on multi-filter support.
	if (art.unbound_expressions.size() > 1) {
		return false;
	}
```

A multi-dimensional point query such as `a = 11 AND b = 24` therefore always runs as a full table scan in the current fork. The coordinate lattice fills this gap with an exact access path: the bounded dimensions pack into one scalar through the mixed-radix closed form, a point query resolves in O(1) arithmetic, and a range box enumerates the matching subspace through the box iterator. This is the ExaVerif pattern applied to the query path, and it replaces both solutions the FIXME proposes. The two ART scan plus intersection keeps the sorted-set overhead and the compound ART keeps the tree descent; the lattice has neither.

The index use threshold shapes the measurement. The settings `index_scan_max_count` (default 2048) and `index_scan_percentage` (default 0.001) restrict the ART path to matches below the maximum of the two. On a ten-million-row table the ART path activates below 10,000 matching rows; a multi-filter query never activates it regardless of selectivity. The profile gate must therefore separate two regimes: the scan-dominated regime above the threshold, and the index regime below it, where the lattice claim is measured against the ART descent and the sorted-set materialization.

### Joint zonemap pruning

The scan path prunes row groups and column segments through per-column minimum and maximum statistics. `RowGroup::CheckZonemap` and `RowGroup::CheckZonemapSegments` in `src/storage/table/row_group.cpp` evaluate each filter column independently:

```duckdb/src/storage/table/row_group.cpp#L716-730
bool RowGroup::CheckZonemap(optional_ptr<ClientContext> context, ScanFilterInfo &filters, idx_t row_start) {
	const auto table_filters = filters.GetTableFilters();
	const auto column_ids = filters.GetColumnIds();
	if (table_filters && column_ids) {
		for (const auto &filter : table_filters->GetMultiColumnFilters()) {
```

A segment passes when each column's interval overlaps the filter, even when no row jointly satisfies every bound. The joint condition is lost. A per-row-group lattice cell set, kept as sparse metadata, tests the query box against the occupied cells in O(1) arithmetic per segment and restores the joint condition. This area sits behind the existing boolean `CheckZonemap` API, so it does not change the scan semantics. It is the lowest-risk integration and the natural carrier for the lattice metadata build.

### Row-id range materialization

The ART scan returns row IDs as a sorted `set<row_t>`, and `DuckIndexScanInitGlobal` copies the set into an arena array before the fetch phase:

```duckdb/src/function/table/table_scan.cpp#L503-519
unique_ptr<GlobalTableFunctionState> DuckIndexScanInitGlobal(ClientContext &context, TableFunctionInitInput &input,
                                                             const TableScanBindData &bind_data, set<row_t> &row_ids,
                                                             unique_ptr<StorageLockKey> vacuum_lock) {
	auto g_state = make_uniq<DuckIndexScanState>(context, input.bind_data.get());
	...
		idx_t row_id_count = 0;
		for (const auto row_id : row_ids) {
			g_state->row_ids[row_id_count++] = row_id;
		}
```

The lattice matching subspace is a small set of contiguous index runs in the row-group offset space. Row IDs materialize as range-compressed start-and-count pairs instead of per-row entries, and the exact path count from the box iterator pre-sizes the output without reallocation. This area complements the access path and carries a smaller but real gain in the fetch phase.

### Virtual lattice columns

The deepest change is positional encoding of the dimension columns. For a table declared as a regular lattice, the dimension values derive from the row position, so the dimension columns need no storage and no per-row evaluation. DuckDB already special-cases such derived columns in `row_id_column_data` and `row_number_column_data` under `src/storage/table`. The scan then reads only the payload columns and reconstructs the dimensions by closed-form arithmetic. This area changes the storage format and requires a storage extension; it is the long-term track.

## The syntagma core upgrade scope

The C++ port under `sw/cpp` provides the primitives the integration reuses: the closed-form `Coord` composition, the collision-free `CoordSpace` direct-address table, the `CoordSet` bit array with set operations, the `CoordCube` grid interpretation, and the `BoundingBoxIter` subspace enumeration. The DuckDB integration exposes three gaps in the port.

The coordinate is fixed at three axes with the 19 by 21 by 28 radices and 11,172 valid states. DuckDB dimensions are arbitrary bounded integer columns with per-dimension extents. The ROOT fork already generalized the closed form to a per-axis mixed radix $(R, L, E)$; the port should adopt that generalization as the core primitive: a mixed-radix multi-dimensional coordinate with per-axis extents and arbitrary dimension count, with closed-form composition, decomposition, and ordering.

The direct-address spaces are fixed at 11,172 slots. The lattice metadata unit for DuckDB is the row group, which holds 122,880 rows, so the occupied-cell set per row group is at most the row-group capacity and independent of the table size. The port needs parameterized or sparse set structures sized per row group, where a dense bitmap stays near 15 KB per dimension set and an interval list covers the sparse case.

The box enumeration iterates uniform base-11172 characters. Range queries over per-dimension extents need a mixed-radix odometer over per-dimension strides, following the lazy-odometer pattern the ExaVerif structural pipeline measured. The upgrade happens after the profile gate shows the gain, in the measured discipline of the precedents.

## The measurement plan

Phase 1 is the profile gate with the installed DuckDB package, no C++ build: a ten-million-row table with two or three bounded integer dimensions and a payload column, then point and range queries at several selectivities. The measurement records the scan cost per query, the zonemap miss rate of the joint condition, and the selectivity at which the index threshold activates. The gate follows the llama.cpp discipline: quantify the incumbent cost before implementing.

Phase 2 is the lattice prototype against the scan and the ART index. The A/B separates the scan-avoidance gain from the lattice-specific gain, because any index beats a scan on selective queries. The prototype covers the multi-filter gap and the joint zonemap pruning; the syntagma core upgrade lands in this phase if the gate supports it.

Phase 3 is the verdict and the extension. If the lattice wins on the measurements, the contribution vehicle is the DuckDB extension system, a table function or storage extension exposing the lattice access path, benchmarked against the stock engine. Parity records a measured negative result and closes the track.

## Status

Planning. The immediate next step is the profile gate with the installed DuckDB package. The syntagma issue is #54 in the `ssccsorg/syntagma` repository, and the analysis lives in this report on the ssccs main branch under the docs exception.

## Boundaries

The lattice addresses bounded integer dimensions with controlled extents; the packed key space is the product of the extents, so the metadata must stay sparse per row group to remain smaller than the data. The DuckDB core is scan-first by design, so the extension path is the realistic contribution vehicle. All results are measured and reported as they are, with no projection ahead of measurement.
